assistant_text:
Here is a concise way to see why they are related but not the same law.

Why they belong to the same family
- Both are conservation statements: they assert that some quantity remains unchanged during a chemical transformation.
- In practice, both help you balance reactions and reason about what can or cannot occur.
- They reflect the same underlying idea that matter is organized into reusable building blocks (atoms) and that transformations rearrange rather than create or destroy matter, at least in ordinary chemical processes.

How they differ
- What is conserved
  - Atom conservation: The number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of a balanced chemical equation. Atoms are simply rearranged.
  - Mass conservation: The total mass (the sum of the masses of all reactants) is the same before and after a reaction. Mass is a bulk property derived from the masses of atoms and their counts.
- What this depends on
  - Atom conservation rests on the existence of atoms as discrete units in chemistry and the idea that chemical reactions do not change the identity or count of atoms, only their bonding and arrangement.
  - Mass conservation rests on additive, measurable mass of substances; in ordinary chemical reactions, adding up atomic masses in the reactants equals the sum in the products to a high precision.
- Domain and limits
  - In standard chemical reactions, both laws hold and are effectively equivalent in practice: balancing atoms automatically ensures mass is balanced.
  - They diverge in more general physics:
    - Nuclear reactions can change the identity of atoms (transmutation) and involve mass changes due to binding energy; total mass is not strictly conserved, though mass-energy is.
    - Modern physics speaks of mass-energy conservation rather than strict mass conservation.
- A practical takeaway
  - You can use atom conservation to balance most chemical equations.
  - Mass conservation is a good cross-check in chemistry, but be aware it has limitations in contexts where energy changes (and relativistic effects) matter.

Summary
- They are both conservation laws and part of the same family of invariants used in chemistry.
- They are not the same law because atom conservation is about counts of discrete building blocks (atoms) in chemical processes, whereas mass conservation is about a bulk property that, in deeper physics, does not remain strictly constant in all processes (mass can convert to energy and vice versa).

task_contract.semantic_unit: Explain why mass conservation and atom conservation belong to the same family but must not be treated as the same law.
